patterns: Winning Shorts in this niche come from channels with 1K-30K subscribers: a sharp question or counter-intuitive claim beats channel size.

Title shapes that break out: 'Why <thing> <surprising verb>?', 'How can <impossible-sounding thing> happen?', 'X vs Y vs Z' size comparisons, 'You've never actually <everyday thing>', 'What if you dropped <object> from space?'.
Length: the biggest science/space hits run 24-60 seconds; history hits are very short (7-60 s). Never pad past 60 s.
Space search demand is steady and low-competition (about 40-45/100): 'facts about space', 'space fun facts', 'facts space' (+162% growth). Use those words naturally in title and description.
Dated hooks win now: upcoming eclipses/sky events of 2027, Starlink/satellite stories, asteroid and dinosaur extinction, dark matter, black holes (TON 618).

findings: Curiosity science beats AI-tool content on this channel: the two best Shorts (space, brain) got 1,689 and 1,110 views; AI prompts/tool tutorials got 21-30 views each.
Best length is 27-32 seconds; the 40+ second Shorts got fewer views.
The 'N facts that sound fake but are true' frame worked for brain (1,110) but not for AI (81): the topic decides, not the frame.
Long videos (4-8 min) got 9-34 views: stay with Shorts.
Likes run about 1-1.5% of views; no Short has comments to speak of yet, so end with a question that is easy to answer in a word.
channel.direction: Make space, physics, brain and Earth-scale curiosity Shorts of 25-35 seconds with one 'impossible but true' claim in the first two seconds. Stop AI-tool/prompt tutorials and phone-tip lists.
channel.visual_level: Cinematic real-photo and NASA footage with one or two big animated numbers or comparisons per Short (the winners were scale and comparison ideas: Space Is Too Big, Walking vs Light). Keep text minimal and large.
